title: Time Management Training and Student Stress

scenes.narration: Can a brief time management training help students feel less stressed and more in control of time during an ongoing semester? This study asked.
The authors begin from a concern in prior research: university students often report stress, and time-related demands are described as a serious problem.
In the paper, time-related demands include high workload, time pressure, and the challenge of self-organized learning in higher education for many students.
The authors say research on time management training effectiveness is scarce, especially intervention studies with student samples and stress outcomes over time.
Their research question was whether training could increase perceived control of time and reduce perceived stress, while perceived, self-reported demands stayed unchanged.
They used a non-equivalent dependent variable design: one trained group, two intended outcomes, and one control variable not expected to change after training.
Forty-eight local undergraduate students began at a medium-sized German university, and 23 completed all questionnaires used in the main analyses reported here.
Among the 23 completers, mean age was 23.30 years, and about half of the participants were female, 52 %, in this sample.
Students attended a 4-hour training in the middle of the semester, in groups of about ten, led by one experienced trainer.
Questionnaires were completed directly before training, 2 weeks after training, and 4 weeks after training, all within the same external context of the semester.
The training focused on prioritizing, goal setting, strategy development, daily planning, and monitoring, drawing on the Häfner and Stock training approach described.
First, students reflected on current academic and extracurricular activities, considered importance for study goals, and tried to define the most important ones.
Next, they defined concrete, challenging, proximal goals with deadlines, then developed steps, priorities, starting plans, and ways around possible obstacles toward goals.
Later, daily planning asked what to do, when, where, and for how long; monitoring checked completed tasks and remaining work each day.
Perceived stress was measured with the tension scale, covering mental fatigue, trouble relaxing, and nervousness; demands covered work amount and external duties.
Perceived control of time included feeling in control, estimating task time correctly, avoiding procrastination, and following one’s plans, as the paper describes.
After training, reported use of time management strategies showed a nearly significant increase at 2 weeks and a significant increase at 4 weeks.
At 2 weeks, the repeated-measurement MANOVA showed a significant overall time effect and significantly less stress measured by tension than before training.
For perceived control of time at 2 weeks, the paper reports no significant increase, only a moderate tendency in the expected direction.
At 4 weeks, the overall time effect was significant, and participants reported less tension and more perceived control of time than before training.
The control variable behaved as hypothesized: perceived, self-reported demands showed no significant changes at either 2 weeks or 4 weeks after training.
Students with no or little prior time management experience seemed to profit more, especially for perceived stress, than students with moderate or some experience.
In the authors’ interpretation, prioritizing, goal setting, and strategy development might give students more orientation, which might reduce stress and foster control.
They also suggest daily planning might help initiate goal-oriented behaviour, while monitoring completed tasks might provide reinforcing information that might affect stress.
Because intended variables changed and demands did not, the authors argue the pattern supports training as the likely cause of changes reported.
Still, they call the study preliminary: the sample was small, dropout was about half, and stronger designs with control groups are improvements.
The takeaway is cautious: time management training might benefit undergraduate students’ well-being, but larger intervention studies are needed for more robust conclusions.
